sessions.title: Welcome to the New World
sessions.subtitle: Terminal, Shell, and Your Dev Environment
sessions.hook: Day one. You wake up in front of a blinking cursor, learn to talk to the machine, and build your first folders and files without touching the mouse.
sideQuestWhy: Day one feels like progress because everything is a first. This page is the loop for the hour when it stops: get one explanation, watch one demonstration, copy it until it runs, then point the same moves at an idea that is yours.

The terminal is the first of about sixty concepts you will be asked to explain in a sentence; this guide is the list, written for the imposter-syndrome moment, and today you can already say the first few: what a terminal is, what a shell is, what `pwd` does.

sessions.title: Your Status Screen
sessions.subtitle: Filesystem Navigation, Pipes, and Permissions
sessions.hook: Yesterday you learned to talk. Today you learn to see: where you are in the tree, what is around you, how to chain commands into combos, and why a file sometimes refuses you.
sideQuestWhy: `ls -R` and `grep -r` walk the filesystem the way this page walks a tree: into a folder, through everything under it, back up, next folder. That order has a name, depth-first, and you will write it yourself in Unit 9; today just recognise the shape in the first picture.

Owner, group, others and read, write, execute is the oldest access-control model in computing, and *Broken Access Control* is the number-one web vulnerability for the same reason `chmod 777` is a bad habit: someone could do something they should not have been allowed to. Read the opening; the code is for Unit 7.

sessions.title: Save Points and Respawns
sessions.subtitle: Git Init, Commit, Branch, Merge
sessions.hook: Three hours of work, one careless edit, everything gone. In a game that never happens, because you saved before the boss. Git is the save system for your code: snapshots you can return to, timelines you can try things in, and a merge that joins the best of both.
sideQuestWhy: A commit holds the hash of its parent and nothing else points forward: `git log` is walking a linked list from the newest node back to the root. Read the opening and the first picture; the `next` pointer there is Fig 2's parent arrow with the direction reversed, and in Unit 9 you will build the structure yourself.

Memento is the save-point pattern written as code: capture an object's whole state so it can be restored later without the outside world knowing what is inside. A commit is a memento of a folder, `.git` is the caretaker, and `git checkout` is the restore. Read the intent and the first diagram; the Java-style class names can wait.

Once a merge commit has two parents the history is no longer a line, it is a graph, which is why the command is called `git log --graph` and why Git can find the shared ancestor of two branches before it merges them. Read what a node and an edge are and look at the first picture; the traversal code is for Unit 9.

sessions.title: Guild Sync
sessions.subtitle: GitHub, Remotes, Pull Requests, and Your Dotfiles
sessions.hook: Everything you have built lives on one laptop. If the laptop dies, the work dies with it. Today the save system goes online: you prove who you are with a key, push your repositories to GitHub, open your first pull request, and ship the project every developer eventually builds, a dotfiles repo that can set up a new machine in one command.
sideQuestWhy: Your SSH key pair is public-key cryptography doing exactly what it is for: a signature anyone can check and only you can make. This page is the catalogue of ways that goes wrong in real systems: weak algorithms, secrets committed to repositories, keys that never rotate. Read the opening and the first example; the rule about never pushing a private key is item one on its list.

`Permission denied (publickey)` and `Hi adventurer-dev!` are the two outcomes of an authentication check, and GitHub chose keys over passwords for the reasons this page catalogues: credential stuffing, reuse, and secrets that cross the wire. Read the opening and the lockout example, and notice that a key never has to be typed anywhere.

You just watched a demonstration: a key, a remote, a push. This page is what to do next. Copy that loop until it works, then use it on a repository that is yours. The skill is coming back tomorrow, not the first green square.

sessions.title: The Skeleton Frame
sessions.subtitle: Semantic HTML and How the Web Works
sessions.hook: Everything you have built so far is a black screen and white text. Today the work becomes something a person can see. A web page is a file a server sends because a browser asked, and HTML is the language that file is written in: a skeleton of named regions, not a programming language, and not a pile of boxes.
sideQuestWhy: Step two of Fig 1, the name becoming an address, is this page. The session only needs you to know the lookup happens before any request; the page is the lookup itself, root then top-level domain then the site's own nameserver, plus the TTL that makes a changed address linger. Read Say this and the four-line walk.

The tree you walked with the live script is the textbook composite: elements contain elements, and a leaf (an img, a piece of text) and a branch (a section, a list) share one node interface, which is why one recursive function could print the whole page. The page names the DOM under SEEN IN. Read the intent and look at the first picture; the class code is for later.

That same walk is a depth-first traversal: finish a region's children before moving to the next region, which is why the printed outline indents. This page is the traversal named and drawn. Read the opening and the first picture; the code that walks a binary tree is the same shape pointed at elements instead of numbers.

sessions.title: Armor and Cosmetics
sessions.subtitle: CSS Fundamentals, the Cascade, and Specificity
sessions.hook: The skeleton from last session is sound, and it looks like a form from 1997. CSS is the armor: a separate file of rules that says which elements look like what. The work today is the system underneath the paint, because a rule that does not apply is almost never a mystery. It lost a fight you can learn to referee.
sideQuestWhy: A selector is a tiny language, and the browser is its interpreter: it reads `nav a:hover` and decides which elements the sentence names. This page's SEEN IN list includes CSS selector matching in querySelector, which is the same match DevTools shows you when a rule is struck through. Read the intent. The grammar-as-classes code is for later.

A class adds a responsibility, color or spacing or a hover, without inventing a new element. Stacking `.card` and `.sale` is the move this page names: same interface, another layer, no SaleCard subclass. Read the intent and the first picture; the HTTP-client wrapping is the same shape pointed at a div.

The Styles panel is a visitor. It walks every rule, keeps the ones that matched, and shows you the winner. PostCSS, which this page names, walks declarations the same way, rule by rule. Read the intent. You already did the walk by hand with the columns in Fig 2.

The gift sites decide every color once, on :root, before a section exists. This is that file: King Chrissy's gold and xoxoshayla's lilac, and the one accent this guide uses instead. Read the two palettes and write the root.
A heading and a pill should already look like the gift sites before you draw a hero. This page is the reset, the container, the skip link, and the eyebrow. Read it after the tokens.

sessions.title: Formation Magic
sessions.subtitle: Flexbox, CSS Grid, and Responsive Design
sessions.hook: The armor is on, and everything is still one column. A navigation bar, a row of cards, a sidebar beside the story, a page that rearranges when the window gets narrow: that is layout. Flexbox handles one direction. Grid handles both. You write the small screen first, and each wider screen adds to it.
sideQuestWhy: A page is a container of containers: the grid holds regions, a region holds a flex row, the row holds links. That is the composite, a tree where a branch and a leaf answer to the same idea of 'a node with children.' The page names the DOM. Read the intent and the first picture; the class code is for later.

Flex or grid is not a rule to memorize, it is a choice with a context, which is the only lesson on this page that survives contact with a real stylesheet. There is no always. Read the mindset section and bring it back to the table in this session: a bar is one axis, a page is two, and a wrapping card row can honestly be either.

grid-template-areas is one door in front of tracks, lines, and placement. You write a picture made of names, and the grid does the bookkeeping. That is a facade: a simpler interface over a subsystem that does not know you simplified it. Read the intent. The order-and-inventory example is the same shape.

The nav on both gift sites is a fixed bar whose underline grows and whose links become a full-screen menu. Flex is the row. The menu is the column. Read the fixed nav before you invent a third layout for links.
The hero is the split you just learned: type in one track, a portrait in the other, the title sized with clamp so the phone and the desktop share one rule. Read the split and write it.
A grid of cards is the auto-fit track from this session, with a hover that lifts the paint and not the layout. Read the link grid and build six of them.

sessions.title: Enchantments
sessions.subtitle: Animations, Transforms, Images, and BEM
sessions.hook: The page is structured, colored, and arranged, and it is still a still picture. A hover that eases, a card that lifts, a spinner that turns, a photograph that fits its frame: motion and fit are how a page tells you it can be touched. The names have to stay readable while you add them, which is what BEM is for.
sideQuestWhy: A modifier is a variation hung on a component that already exists: quest-card and quest-card--featured, not a second component. That is the decorator: same interface, another layer. Read the intent and the first picture. The wrapping example is the same move as a modifier class.

Rest, hover, and pressed are three states of one button, and each state has its own declarations. The transition is only the trip between them. Read the intent. The class diagram is that idea pointed at a control instead of a quest card.

A block is a tree of named parts: the card contains a badge, a title, a description, a reward. The composite page is a tree where a part and a whole are addressed the same way. Read the intent and look at the first picture. Fig 4 on this session is that tree with the names written on it.
object-fit and a shared aspect ratio are how the gift-site galleries stay even when the photographs do not. Read Pictures and crop six images on purpose.

The loader, the marquee, and the scroll reveal are the motion from this session, written as classes. Reduced motion turns them off. Read Motion and add one reveal. The CSS half is for now; the part that toggles classes with a script waits for Session 3.5.

The gate, the cursor, and the mute button are the same idea: the stylesheet holds the look, the script only adds a class. The cursor is limited to a fine pointer. Read the CSS half now and build the static shell; the click, focus, and sound half is a Session 3.5 return trip.

sessions.title: The Character Sheet Forge
sessions.subtitle: Build and Deploy Your Landing Page
sideQuestWhy: The page is a tree: sections hold cards, cards hold a title and a body, and the Composite sheet is the name for treating a card and the grid around it the same way; read the idiomatic shape, nested data plus one recursive function, and you will recognise the DOM you just wrote.

A BEM modifier such as a secondary button adds one behaviour to a base without rewriting it, which is the Decorator idea in a stylesheet; read the higher-order-function shape so the pattern has a name before Unit 3 gives you functions to wrap.

The two widths where this landing page simplifies: the hero stacks, the nav swaps from a column to a row, the grid collapses to one column. Read Breakpoints and check 390 and 1440 in the device toolbar before you enable Pages.

Assembly is the landing page you are shipping, written in the order of the two stylesheets; read it last, then compare it against the dtc-landing repository and your own index.html, and name the decisions where yours differs.
sessions.hook: Five sessions of skeleton, armor, formation and motion become one page with your name on it, and today it goes on the internet at a URL you can send to anyone. Then you prove the page a visitor gets is the page you built: on a phone, from the keyboard, with every path resolving under the prefix GitHub gives you.

sessions.title: Mana Basics
sessions.subtitle: Variables, Data Types, Operators, and Control Flow
sessions.hook: Your first mana bar: where values live, the seven kinds they come in, and how a program picks a road.
sideQuestWhy: The full table behind fig. 5: ===, == and Object.is, the falsy six, typeof, and every coercion rule as runnable asserts.
Why 0.1 + 0.2 is not 0.3, how to round and format, parseInt versus Number, and the limits of the number type.
Everything the template literal did not cover: indexing, slicing, splitting, the immutability trap.
var versus let versus const, the classic loop bug, and hoisting explained from scope up; read this one after Session 3.2 if it feels early.

sessions.title: Spell Crafting
sessions.subtitle: Functions, Scope, Closures, and Array Methods
sessions.hook: Write the incantation once, name it, and cast it anywhere; then learn why some spells remember.
sideQuestWhy: The reference sheet for today: scope, the backpack, the classic loop, and function hoisting as runnable asserts.
Every array method in one place, mutating versus copying, 2D grids, and the aliasing trap behind the shallow-copy demo.
Destructuring, spread, rest and the copy table in full, including when structuredClone is the right tool.
The comparator function sort wants, why sort mutates, and how to sort by two keys without destroying the input.

sessions.title: Objects and Orcs
sessions.subtitle: Object-Oriented Programming in JavaScript
sessions.hook: One blueprint, five hundred knights, and the word that keeps losing its character.
sideQuestWhy: The reference sheet for today: class syntax, the four rules of this, and the prototype chain as runnable asserts.
Everything about reading and copying objects: destructuring, spread, Object.entries, shallow versus deep copies.
The closure that made the factory's secret private, explained from scope and hoisting up.
The design pattern named after today's mechanism: cloning from an existing object instead of a class.
What createHero grows into when the kind of object depends on the input.

sessions.title: Casting on the World
sessions.subtitle: The DOM, Events, and Dynamic Interfaces
sessions.hook: Your JavaScript leaves the training dungeon: select a corner of the page, change it, and make it answer when someone clicks.
sideQuestWhy: addEventListener is the Observer pattern with the browser as the subject: attach, detach, notify. See it written out in plain objects.
The quest board's controller, one handler that coordinates the form, the list and the counter, is a Mediator; this sheet names the shape and its trade-off.
A button click that becomes an object with execute() and undo() is the Command pattern, and the Quest Log's stretch goals want it.
The Quest class meets `this` inside event handlers; this sheet is where arrow functions versus methods stops being a mystery.

sessions.title: The Arena
sessions.subtitle: Build and Deploy Your Browser Game
sessions.hook: Project day. Everything from Unit 3 becomes one playable, deployed game with a URL you can hand to anyone.
sideQuestWhy: idle → playing → over is a state machine, and every `if (winner) return` guard is one of its transitions; this sheet shows each state as an object, which is where your game goes when the ifs pile up.

A `Game` class whose `start()` runs the fixed sequence and whose `buildBoard()` is filled in by each specific game is the Template Method; this sheet names the parts so you can explain your own architecture.

`randomInt` is `Math.floor(Math.random() * (max - min + 1)) + min`, and every off-by-one in a dice roll or a timer lives in that line; this sheet covers floor versus round versus trunc, parsing, and why `parseInt` of a label is NaN.
Project day is where a copied demonstration stops being enough. This page says copying is the third step. The fourth is your own idea, and it will not work the first time. Stay with that hour.

sessions.title: The Runtime Beyond the Browser
sessions.subtitle: What Node.js is, and what Express is
sessions.hook: JavaScript leaves the page. Node is the runtime that runs it on a machine, and Express is the small library that turns that machine into a server.
sideQuestWhy: Express is a facade: a small, pleasant surface over Node's http module. This sheet names that shape, a simple interface in front of a messier subsystem.
The Proxy pattern is the other half of the word you will meet again in Unit 6. Read it now so 'the server' and 'the thing in front of the server' are already different objects in your head.

sessions.title: The Listening Door
sessions.subtitle: Create a server with Express
sessions.hook: One process, one port, and a stack of functions. Today you build the door: routes, middleware, and an error handler that actually answers.
sideQuestWhy: Middleware is a chain of responsibility: each function does its part and calls next, or it ends the response. This sheet is that pattern without Express around it.
The app object is still the facade from last session. Come back to it once you have seen the chain it hides.

sessions.title: The Counter's Three Laws
sessions.subtitle: REST, MVC, and JSON
sessions.hook: A URL is not a page. It is a noun, the method is the verb, and the body is JSON. MVC is how you keep those three from collapsing into one file.
sideQuestWhy: REST is one choice among API styles. This sheet puts it next to GraphQL and gRPC so you can say why a quest board wants resources and verbs, not a single query language.
A controller that coordinates the model and the response, and does not let them talk past it, is a mediator. The sheet shows the shape you are about to write by hand.

sessions.title: The Vault
sessions.subtitle: MongoDB and databases in general
sessions.hook: A variable dies when the process dies. A database is the other kind of memory: documents on disk, queried by fields, shared by every request.
sideQuestWhy: MongoDB is one answer to SQL versus NoSQL. Read the trade-off before you treat documents as 'just easier tables.'
The unique hero and the find-by-id you write next session are indexes. This sheet is the cost of having them and the cost of not having them.

sessions.title: The Vault Keeper
sessions.subtitle: Mongoose and ODMs
sessions.hook: MongoDB will store whatever you hand it. Mongoose is the keeper at the door: a schema, a model, validators, and queries that return promises.
sideQuestWhy: schema.index and unique: true become indexes. Go read what an index costs on a write, now that you are about to add one.
An ODM is not a different database. MongoDB is still a document store. This sheet keeps that line from blurring once the API feels like objects.

sessions.title: The Paper Ledger
sessions.subtitle: Server-rendered HTML with Express, Mongoose, and INDUCES
sessions.hook: Before React, the server sends the page. Seven routes, one resource, plain HTML and CSS. The name of the seven is INDUCES.
sideQuestWhy: The controller is a mediator between the Mongoose model and the HTML you send. The sheet is the pattern with the participants named.
method-override and the body parser are middleware in a chain. Order is the whole bug. The chain-of-responsibility sheet is why calling next is the design, not a quirk.

sessions.title: The Courier
sessions.subtitle: A RESTful API that returns JSON
sessions.hook: The same quests, with the HTML left behind. The client sends JSON and receives JSON. Status codes do the talking that a redirect used to do.
sideQuestWhy: You just chose a resource style on purpose. The API-design sheet is the argument you should be able to repeat.
The documents are still documents. If a teammate asks why this is not a table with joins, you want the SQL-versus-NoSQL page in reach.

The courier is a JSON API in Express. The Python track builds the same todos API in Django in five short pages, and it answers the same curl commands; read its index to see the shape of a second language before you decide whether to walk it.

Go is the other end of the spectrum from JavaScript: typed, compiled, one binary. Its track ends with the same todos contract you just spoke to with curl, so you can compare a Go handler with the courier's route line by line.

sessions.title: Seals and Signets
sessions.subtitle: bcrypt, JWT, and authentication with curl
sessions.hook: No React yet. A password becomes a hash, a login returns a signed token, and the next request carries that token in a header. The server is the only thing that believes it.
sideQuestWhy: Authentication is who you are. Authorization is what you may do. This sheet separates them before the token makes them feel like one thing.
Authentication failures are an OWASP category of their own: weak hashes, missing expiry, tokens in logs. Read the fixes next to the code you just wrote.
Broken access control is the next bug, and it will not show up in curl if you only call the route as yourself. The sheet's first case is calling it as someone else.

sessions.title: The Illusionist's Primer
sessions.subtitle: React, the basics
sessions.hook: The page stops being a string you send once. React is a description of the UI from state. Change the state, and React updates the DOM.
sideQuestWhy: A screen made of components that contain components is the composite pattern. The sheet is the tree you are already drawing.
onClick is the observer pattern with React as the subject. Read the subscribe and notify language so the handler stops feeling like magic.
The cheatsheet is the reference card for the hooks and patterns this session introduces; keep it open while you build the primer and come back to it whenever a hook's signature slips.

sessions.title: The Second Circle
sessions.subtitle: Effects, forms, and shared state
sessions.hook: State inside one component is not enough. Today the data lives above the children that need it, and effects are reserved for synchronizing with something outside React.
sideQuestWhy: Loading, empty, error, and ready are states of the screen. The State pattern sheet is what this becomes when the ifs pile up.
The effect that subscribes, and the cleanup that unsubscribes, is the observer pattern with a return function. Read the cleanup as detach.

sessions.title: The Quest Slate
sessions.subtitle: A React todo on your API, with JWT auth
sessions.hook: The pieces meet. A todo list in React, a JSON API in Express, a token from the login you already proved with curl. The screen waits for the server before it says saved.
sideQuestWhy: The UI hiding the delete button is not the control. Call the route as the other user. This sheet is that bug, written out.
Login established identity. The todo route has to decide authorization separately, per record. Re-read the split before you check only that a token exists.

The React guide in the library builds a todo client against the shared todos API, the same list, show, create, edit, delete flow as the slate, with the finished app deployed; read it after today to see the same shape without the login.

sessions.title: The Second Contract
sessions.subtitle: Another CRUD app with the same JWT auth
sessions.hook: You have built this shape once, with the notes open. Today you build it again, a spellbook instead of a todo list, and the notes stay closed until something actually breaks.
sideQuestWhy: The API your React app calls is a facade over Mongoose. If the second app's client knows about schemas, the facade has leaked. The sheet is the line.
You will be tempted to loosen the password rules to make the demo easier. The authentication-failures page is the argument against that shortcut.

sessions.title: Blood Oaths
sessions.subtitle: Many-to-many relationships with Express and Mongoose
sessions.hook: A spell has one owner. A party has many members, and a member stands in many parties. That second sentence is a different shape, and Mongoose will not invent it for you.
sideQuestWhy: The compound unique index on party plus member is the indexing page in miniature. Read the write cost now, while the collection is small enough to feel free.
A join collection is the document version of a join table. The SQL-versus-NoSQL sheet is how you explain that to someone who only knows rows.

sessions.title: The Guild Hall
sessions.subtitle: Messages, inventory, and a small social world
sessions.hook: The unit's project. Accounts you already know how to seal, an inbox between them, and a pack of potions, weapons, and armor. Not every link is many-to-many. You have to say which is which.
sideQuestWhy: The inbox is broken access control waiting to happen: change the id, read someone else's mail. The sheet's first example is this request.
A pack that contains items, and an item that is itself a simple leaf, is a composite if you later nest kits inside kits. Read the pattern before you reach for recursion.
Holdings will be queried by owner constantly. The index on owner is the difference between a pack that opens and a pack that scans every row you have ever stored.

Every backend guide in the library serves one contract and every frontend guide consumes it; the hall is your first client-plus-server pair, and this index shows you can mix any of the four clients with any of the eight servers.

sessions.title: Awakening the Cheat Skill
sessions.subtitle: The RTTPOC Prompt Framework
sideQuestWhy: The six lines become reflex only after the long stretch of writing a rubric before every run, which is the country between level-ups the grit sheet describes.
A prompt with one task and one responsibility is the single-responsibility principle applied to a chat window; a task with two verbs is two prompts.
sessions.hook: Four units in, you have been casting at the model without an incantation. Today you learn one: Role, Task, Tone, Purpose, Output, Constraints, and a rubric that says whether the answer passed.

sessions.title: Advanced Incantations
sessions.subtitle: Prompt Patterns, Context Windows, and Iteration
sideQuestWhy: Rerunning the five old statuses after every revision, when the new output already looks fine, is the effort the grit sheet says to count twice.
A template whose examples can be swapped to change the behavior while the six lines stay fixed is the strategy pattern with the examples as the strategies.
sessions.hook: The six lines stay. Today you stack three techniques on them: examples from your own handlers, reasoning before writing, and prompts chained so one answer is the next one's context. The hall gets an unread count, built in the chat and verified with curl.

sessions.title: Summoned Familiars
sessions.subtitle: Claude Code, Cursor, and Agentic Workflows
sideQuestWhy: An agent that can add a package is a supply-chain door, which is why Do not add packages is in every brief and in CLAUDE.md.
Reading a diff you could have accepted with one key, every time, is the discipline the grit sheet is about.
sessions.hook: The model stops answering in a tab and starts editing files. Today you install one agent, give it a file of facts it reads before every task, put a branch under it, and let it make one scoped change to the hall that you review line by line and can revert completely.

sessions.title: Cheat Skill Trials
sessions.subtitle: Rebuild a Feature at 10x Speed
sideQuestWhy: Timing the review and the repair honestly, and rerunning seven cases you already believe pass, is grit with a stopwatch on it.
A handler whose one database operation decides the outcome is single responsibility applied to a route, and the rebuild is judged on whether it kept that shape.
sessions.hook: The trial. Pick one feature of the hall you built by hand, write its acceptance cases down, delete it on a branch, and have the agent rebuild it to the same contract while a clock runs. The number you get is the number you get; the log is the evidence, and main gets the merge.

sessions.title: Claiming Territory
sessions.subtitle: Cloud Machines, SSH, and Server Setup
sideQuestWhy: The deploy account with sudo and the ed25519 key in authorized_keys are authentication and authorization in their smallest working form.
A cloud-init drop-in that silently keeps password login on is a security misconfiguration you only catch by reading sshd -T instead of the file.
sessions.hook: Everything you have built runs on your laptop. Today you rent a Linux machine in a data center, reach it with the key you already own, close every door but three, and leave it waiting for the guild hall.

sessions.title: The Gatekeeper
sessions.subtitle: Nginx, Reverse Proxies, and Process Management
sideQuestWhy: The location /api/ block forwarding to 127.0.0.1 is a reverse proxy in its narrowest form, and the sheet explains why the client never sees the upstream.
The pm2 restart counter and the three log files you located are the first instruments of observability, and the sheet names what to watch next.
sessions.hook: Your server has an address and nothing answering it. Today Nginx takes the public door, a Node process waits behind it on a loopback port, and pm2 brings that process back after a crash and after a reboot.

sessions.title: The Teleportation Network
sessions.subtitle: DNS, Domains, and SSL Certificates
sideQuestWhy: The resolver walk from root to your registrar's nameservers, and the TTL that keeps an old answer alive, are the DNS sheet applied to your own name.
A certificate presented for the wrong name, or one left to expire, is a cryptographic failure the security sheet catalogs, and openssl s_client is how you see it.
sessions.hook: Nobody will type your IP address. Today you register a name, point it at the droplet with one A record, and let certbot fetch a certificate so the browser shows a lock instead of a warning.

sessions.title: Opening the World Gate
sessions.subtitle: Deploy Your Full Stack App to the Internet
sideQuestWhy: pm2 logs, the Nginx access and error logs, and the restart counter are the observability sheet's signals, and the deploy script's smoke lines are its first check.
One droplet running one process is where the availability sheet's arithmetic starts, so read it knowing exactly which single thing your hall depends on.
An 'allow access from anywhere' entry in the Atlas network list, or a database bound to 0.0.0.0, is the security misconfiguration sheet in a single checkbox.
sessions.hook: The server has a name, a lock, and a placeholder page. Today the guild hall moves in: a cloud database, a .env Node reads on the server, hall-api under pm2 on 4100, the Vite build behind Nginx, and a deploy script you can run again.

sessions.title: Sparring Grounds
sessions.subtitle: Jest, Unit Testing, and the TDD Mindset
sideQuestWhy: Every test you keep is a trade-off between the confidence it buys and the seconds it costs on every run, and the trade-offs page is the vocabulary for saying which claims in the dojo earn their place.
A suite that has only ever been green is a first attempt, and the long-return page is about coming back to the red run you did not want to see and reading it until it makes sense.
sessions.hook: The guild hall is live and you have clicked through every screen. Nothing proves it except your memory. Today you write the first test that can fail, watch it fail on purpose, and learn why that red run is the whole point.

sessions.title: Dungeon Trials
sessions.subtitle: Supertest, API Testing, and Integration Tests
sideQuestWhy: The Supertest files are the executable form of the contract the API-design sheet argues about, one it block per status, so read the REST section with messages.test.js open.
Ivo's 403 on Sera's letter is the broken-access-control case from the OWASP page, now checked by a machine instead of remembered by you; the sheet's first example is that request.
sessions.hook: You proved the inbox by hand in 4-15 and wrote four statuses in a note. Today those four lines become four tests that send real requests through the real router into a database that exists only to be wiped.

sessions.title: The Gauntlet
sessions.subtitle: Playwright, E2E Testing, and CI Basics
sideQuestWhy: A Playwright trace with a screenshot at the moment of failure is observability for a test the way logs and spans are observability for a server; read the page with show-report open on a red run.
The first red Actions run, read line by line until the cause is named, is the kind of return the long-return page is written for.
sessions.hook: Nobody uses the hall with curl. Sera uses the page. Today a browser you never touch logs in as Sera and reads Bran's letter, and then GitHub runs that same journey, and every Jest file, on a machine you will never see.

sessions.title: Clearing the Training Dungeon
sessions.subtitle: Build a Real Test Suite
sideQuestWhy: The vulnerability names on the quick-reference sheet are the first column of a risk table like TESTPLAN.md; read it to find a promise the hall makes that your table does not yet name.
A report that says what was observed, against what, and what was only checked by hand is the same discipline the observability page applies to a running service.
sessions.hook: Green is not the same as safe. Today you list what would actually hurt a person using the hall, give each risk a test at the cheapest layer that can catch it, prove the suite from a clean clone, merge add-tests into main through a pull request, and write a report that says exactly what was and was not checked.

sessions.title: Listening at the Tavern
sessions.subtitle: User Research, Interviews, and Empathy Maps
sideQuestWhy: The one-breath definitions are how you answer an interviewee who asks what you actually build, in one sentence, so the warm-up never turns into a pitch.
Recruiting five strangers and getting three to say yes is the kind of week where nothing seems to move; read the grit story before the third unanswered message.
sessions.hook: The guild hall is built. Nobody asked for it. Today you pick the capstone idea in one afternoon, open its repo, write seven questions that cannot be answered with a polite lie, and book the people who will answer them.

sessions.title: The Quest Board
sessions.subtitle: User Stories, Backlogs, and Prioritization
sideQuestWhy: Single Responsibility is INVEST's 'small' said about code: a story that touches four modules is a story to split, and the page gives you the smell test for spotting it.

RICE and ICE are two interchangeable scoring strategies behind one score(story) call; the Strategy page shows that shape, and the model on this page is a plain object map of functions selected by key.
sessions.hook: An idea sentence and one practice interview become a backlog: fifteen to twenty user stories, each tagged evidence or assumption, acceptance examples for the top five, a MoSCoW cut, RICE scores, and a board with four columns where the capstone will be built.

sessions.title: Guild Operations
sessions.subtitle: Agile, SCRUM, Sprints, and Retros
sideQuestWhy: A sprint is a promise to yourself with a date on it, and the grit story's training circle is the same plan, inspect, adapt loop told as fiction.
Open/Closed and Dependency Inversion are what make a story Independent on the board: if finishing card four means reopening card two, the SOLID page names the coupling to cut before you estimate.
sessions.hook: A board on the wall does not clear dungeons. Today every Must story gets a size, the backlog becomes the four sprints Unit 12 actually runs, Sprint 1 gets a goal that fits, and you run your first retrospective on the work you already did in Unit 7.

sessions.title: Field Work
sessions.subtitle: Real User Interviews and Sprint Planning
sideQuestWhy: Three interviews that disagree with your idea are the plateau the grit story is about; the move is to write the finding down and keep going, not to recruit friendlier people.
Interface Segregation is the Sprint 1 goal in code form: the first increment exposes one thin path a tester can walk, not every method the finished product will have.
sessions.hook: Three real people have talked to you. Today their words become a combined empathy map, a set of insights with counts instead of adjectives, a backlog revised line by line with a reason for every change, and the product spec that Unit 12 opens on its first morning.

sessions.title: Ancient Runes
sessions.subtitle: TypeScript Fundamentals and Type Safety
sideQuestWhy: The parser you wrote checks that an id is a string; the next check it needs is that the string has a shape, and the regex sheet is how you say what shape without a second pass of ifs.

An interface is a contract a caller can depend on without reading the implementation, which is the dependency-inversion idea in the SOLID sheet; read it to put a name on what Quest and Chest<T> already do.
sessions.hook: JavaScript lets a typo ride all the way to production. Today you add a compiler that refuses, build a parser that turns unknown JSON into a type you can trust, and learn the two ways Node 24 runs a .ts file.

sessions.title: Trial of Blades
sessions.subtitle: Arrays, Objects, Big O, and Core Data Structures
sideQuestWhy: The Big O sheet is the growth vocabulary on one page; read it after you have pasted your bench output, so each class on the sheet has a number from your machine beside it.
Space is the column of the complexity table most people leave blank; the spatial complexity sheet is the half of the trade a Set makes when it replaces includes.
The arrays pattern sheet catalogues the operations whose costs you just measured; read it to see which array methods hide a loop the way shift does.
sessions.hook: A lookup that takes a millisecond at a thousand rows takes six seconds at a hundred thousand. Today you measure that on your own machine, learn to say why, and build the three structures that make the shape of the growth a choice instead of a surprise.

sessions.title: Trial of Wits
sessions.subtitle: Algorithm Patterns and Whiteboard Practice
sideQuestWhy: The which-pattern-when sheet is the table of conditions this session kept asking you to say out loud before choosing a pattern; use it to check the condition column of your ALGORITHMS.md.

Two pointers only works under a rule that guarantees nothing valid is skipped, usually a sort; the two-pointers sheet lists the inputs that break it, which are the cases your oracle test should generate.
The sliding-window sheet shows the window with negative numbers, the input that makes the pattern give a confident wrong answer; read it before you decide a problem is a window problem.
sessions.hook: A pattern is not a trick to memorize. It is what the structure of the input allows. Today you write the slow version first, keep it as the oracle, and let it prove that the fast version you wrote next gives the same answers.

sessions.title: Grand Architecture
sessions.subtitle: System Design Fundamentals
sideQuestWhy: The interview-framework sheet is this document compressed into forty-five minutes out loud; after you have written section 4, try saying it in five, and notice which hop you cannot defend.
The back-of-the-envelope sheet holds the reference numbers behind section 2; treat them as starting guesses to replace with your own inputs, and cite the ones you kept.
The caching sheet is the four questions you owe before a cache goes in section 3: the source of truth, the key, how long it may lie, and what deletes it.
sessions.hook: Your product spec says what the capstone does. Today you write the document that says how it will hold up: a workload you estimated, boxes you can defend, one request traced through them, one failure walked through, and one decision recorded with its reasons.

sessions.title: The Runesmith's Forge
sessions.subtitle: TypeScript Conversion and Design Doc
sideQuestWhy: The read helpers and the HttpError class gave each handler one responsibility and one error type; the SOLID sheet is the vocabulary for saying why that made the handlers easier to type.
The digital-mansion primer is the long form of the design document you have now written twice; read it to see where ADR-2 sits in a full system description.
ADR-2 has a consequences section, and the trade-offs sheet is the vocabulary for writing it as costs and benefits rather than preferences.
sessions.hook: The guild hall works and has tests. Today you convert it to TypeScript in place, one boundary at a time, with the Unit 7 suite as the proof that nothing changed, and you record why the capstone will not get the same treatment.

sessions.title: Barrier Magic
sessions.subtitle: OWASP, Input Validation, and Secrets Management
sideQuestWhy: Broken access control is the one failure no validation chain can fix, because the clean payload came from the wrong person; read the IDOR and deny-by-default sections and then look at every route in the capstone that reads an id from the URL.
Injection is the category the $gt login body belongs to; read the NoSQL section with rejectOperators open beside it and the SQL section so the pattern has a name outside Mongo.
The quick reference is the glossary for the threat model's rows; read the IDOR, NoSQL injection, and JWT entries tonight and keep the page open while you fill in docs/threat-model.md.
sessions.hook: The capstone gets its first line of code today, copied from the hall you already trust, and then it gets a barrier: every body validated into a shape you chose, headers Helmet sets for you, a limiter on the login door, and a process that refuses to start without its secrets.

sessions.title: Sealed Gates
sessions.subtitle: Stripe, Paid APIs, Webhooks, and Rate Limits
sideQuestWhy: Idempotency is the proper name for claim-then-flip: read the sheet with routes/webhooks.js open and say which write is the claim, which is the conditional transition, and why a retry after a crash between them is still safe.

Rate limiting on the checkout route is about what key a limiter should count once there is more than one process; read the token-bucket section and note in docs/payments.md that today's counter is per process.

Software or data integrity failures is the OWASP category an unsigned webhook belongs to, and the trusting-client-state section is the success URL that unlocked access; read both before you fill in the webhook row of the threat model.
sessions.hook: The capstone takes its first payment today, in test mode, on a checkout page Stripe hosts. Your server picks the price, Stripe sends a signed event, and an order flips from pending to paid exactly once, no matter how many times the same event arrives.

sessions.title: Binding the Great Spirits
sessions.subtitle: LLM APIs, Safe Integration, and Cost Control
sideQuestWhy: Insecure design is the category a feature that lets model output grant a role belongs to; read the business-logic and double-spend sections and compare the budget's conditional write with the race they describe.
Rate limiting is the second limiter the AI routes get next session, keyed by user rather than address; read the sheet now so the keyGenerator choice is a decision and not a default.
Observability is how you will answer what the feature cost last week without opening the provider's dashboard; read the correlation-id section and decide which id every ai log line should carry.
sessions.hook: The capstone gets its one AI feature today: a route that sends a bounded document to Claude from the server, streams the answer back over SSE, treats the document as data rather than orders, and reserves a slice of the user's daily token budget before it spends a single one.

sessions.title: Warding the Kingdom
sessions.subtitle: Add Payments and AI to Your Capstone
sideQuestWhy: The quick reference is the glossary for the audit's Inventory and Must rows; walk its entries against your routes once more before you write GO at the bottom.
Idempotency is the Must row about duplicates said properly; reread the trade-offs section and write in Known gaps what the claim does not cover, such as refunds and async_payment_failed.
Observability turns railway logs from a scroll into a question you can ask; read the correlation-id section and make every webhook and ai log line carry an id you can search for.
sessions.hook: Today the capstone goes live. You write the security audit with a piece of evidence beside every line, put a second limiter and an off switch on the AI routes, and deploy the API, the page, and a database to Railway so that from next session on the capstone is a URL and not a folder.

sessions.title: Rallying the Villagers
sessions.subtitle: Crowdfunding, Community Rounds, and Pre-Sales
sideQuestWhy: The pre-sale model is a back-of-the-envelope calculation: gross, minus fees, minus delivery, minus refunds, and a per-unit margin that sets the break-even count.
Deciding to raise nothing for the next milestone is the long-return choice, and this session treats it as a legitimate answer rather than a failure.
sessions.hook: Your capstone is live and takes test payments. Before anyone hands you money, you decide whether you need it at all, and you model what a pre-sale leaves in the bank after fees, delivery, and refunds.

sessions.title: The Noble Houses
sessions.subtitle: Angel Investors, SAFEs, and Term Sheets
sideQuestWhy: A cap table is shares first and percentages derived, the same envelope discipline: each stage must sum to 100 or a holder is missing.
Walking away from a term sheet that funds six months and costs six years is the long-return decision this session rehearses on a fictional page.
sessions.hook: A noble offers gold for a share of the treasure. Today you read the post-money SAFE, run four conversion scenarios until the arithmetic is yours, and find the red flags in a one-page term sheet before you ever see a real one.

sessions.title: The Royal Court
sessions.subtitle: Venture Capital, Pitch Decks, and the Raise
sideQuestWhy: Fund return, exit value from a stake percentage, and a bottom-up market are three envelope calculations this session runs before any slide is written.
An honest SOM often comes out small, and the long-return mindset is what lets you say so on slide 5 instead of borrowing a headline number.
sessions.hook: A venture fund's arithmetic decides what it can invest in before it ever sees your deck. Today you run that arithmetic, decide honestly whether your capstone fits, and start the twelve slides around the product you already deployed.

sessions.title: War Council
sessions.subtitle: Pitch Deck and Financial Narrative Workshop
sideQuestWhy: runway.js is a back-of-the-envelope model made explicit: inputs at the top, one subtraction per month, and the month cash goes below zero as the answer.
Scoring a second take honestly after fixing three GROWs is the long-return habit; a first take described generously teaches nothing.
sessions.hook: No new theory. You build the month-by-month cash model, let it overrule the slides it disagrees with, record the five-minute pitch against your live product, and score it yourself with the questions an investor would ask.

sessions.title: Sprint 1 — Foundation
sessions.subtitle: Core Features and Architecture
sideQuestWhy: SOLID gives you the words for the question you asked of every box in the architecture record today: what breaks if this is deleted, and what is it the only thing responsible for.

The system-design primer is where the client, server, and persistence boundaries you reconciled against the live URL were first drawn, and it is the sheet to reread before you defend each one on demo day.
sessions.hook: Your capstone already exists, already runs, and is already deployed. Sprint 1 is the day you stop guessing which Must-haves are finished and prove it, one slice at a time, against the plan you wrote in Unit 8.

sessions.title: Sprint 2 — Build
sessions.subtitle: Feature Completion and Integration
sideQuestWhy: The service module you wrapped around the AI and Stripe calls, returning your own shape with four fixtures behind it, is the Adapter pattern with its name on.
The FLOW table and the transition function are the State pattern reduced to a lookup, and the sheet shows what to do when four states become nine.
The REST, GraphQL, and gRPC comparison is the longer answer to why your route returns { summary } instead of the provider's payload, and what the contract between client and server is for.
sessions.hook: The Must-haves agree with the plan. Sprint 2 builds the Should-haves that survived the cut and gives the core flow one status string that decides what every button does, so a double click, a failed save, and an empty list each do exactly one thing.

sessions.title: Sprint 3 — Harden
sessions.subtitle: Testing, Security, and Deployment
sideQuestWhy: The vulnerability quick reference is the longer list behind the five requests you sent today as the wrong user, with the names reviewers use for each one.
Observability is what to read before you decide what broken will mean on the live URL once nobody is watching the terminal, which the handoff in 12-5 will ask you to write down.
Availability and the nines turns your three recovery numbers, backup age, restore time, and data at risk, into the language a reviewer expects for them.
sessions.hook: No new features today. Sprint 3 freezes one commit, runs the whole test tree against exactly that commit, attacks the ownership rules with a second account, restores a backup somewhere disposable, and redeploys with the path you already own.

sessions.title: Sprint 4 — Polish
sessions.subtitle: Final Touches and Presentation Prep
sideQuestWhy: Grit is for the hour when you have watched yourself say um nine times on the rehearsal take and want to skip the second read-through.
The State sheet is the reason the four sentences on every screen were a lookup on the existing status string instead of four new booleans.
sessions.hook: The candidate is live. Sprint 4 hunts bugs as a stranger, gives every screen its loading, empty, and success sentences, adds the 404 page, writes a README someone can run from, and records the five-minute demo for the first time so you can watch it back before it counts.

sessions.title: Coronation Day
sessions.subtitle: Demo Day, Launch, and Your Next Quest
sideQuestWhy: Knowing what you are talking about is the standard the five written answers are held to: each one points at a file, or it is a belief rather than a thing you built.
Grit is for the week after the crown, when the streak has no audience and the experiment in docs/next-quest.md has a date on it.
Observability is what the who-watches-it line in the handoff grows into if the product stays live and a stranger signs up next month.
sessions.hook: Twenty weeks after the blinking cursor, you record the demo that counts on the live URL, answer the five questions a reviewer would ask, score your own capstone against a hundred points, and hand the product to the person who will run it next: you.
